# AccessBay Documentation

Canonical: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/

This file contains the main public documentation content in a machine-readable text format.

## AccessBay: sell software from your own WordPress site
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/
Description: Sell plugins, themes and software from your own WordPress site. AccessBay issues licences, delivers updates to paying customers only, and keeps the customer relationship yours.

<div class="about">

## Sell your software. Skip the busywork.

You build the product. AccessBay handles what happens after the sale. A customer pays, and their licence key is created and
emailed. They refund, and the licence is taken back. Nobody has to touch it.

You sell from your own site, so there is no marketplace in the middle. You keep your revenue, and you know exactly who your customers are.

</div>

## Built for people who sell software and digital products

<div class="card-grid audience-grid">
	<Card icon="code" variant="audience" title="Plugin and theme developers">
		Every buyer gets a licence key and automatic updates. You ship your plugin and skip building a licensing system.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="briefcase" variant="audience" title="Agencies and freelancers">
		Sell to clients from a site you control. See who bought what, and which sites are using it.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="shopping-cart" variant="audience" title="Store owners selling software">
		Add licences and protected updates to the store you already run. Keep your products, prices and checkout.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="package" variant="audience" title="Software vendors">
		Build licence checks and updates into your own plugin or theme, so buyers never leave it. The SDK is in beta.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="terminal" variant="audience" title="Teams with their own tools">
		Hook AccessBay into the tools you already use. Each connection can do only what you allow.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="package" variant="audience" title="Resellers and agency partners">
		Buy a block of licences once and hand them out to your own clients. Planned as a Pro feature; on the roadmap.
	</Card>
</div>

## Why sellers choose AccessBay

<div class="card-grid reason-grid">
	<Card icon="house" variant="reason" title="Your customers stay yours">
		Orders, emails and customer details live on your own site. No platform stands between you and your buyers.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="key-round" variant="reason" title="Licensing that just works">
		Set how many sites each licence covers. Every sale gets a key, and every refund takes it back.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="plug" variant="reason" title="Keep your WooCommerce store">
		A paid order creates the licence. A refund or dispute takes it back. Your store stays as it is.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="shield-check" variant="reason" title="Updates only buyers can get">
		Only paying customers get your updates. Download links expire, so a shared link stops working.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="mail-check" variant="reason" title="Licence emails that arrive">
		If one mail provider fails, the email goes out through another. You get an alert, so no buyer is left waiting.
	</Card>
	<Card icon="scale" variant="reason" title="Open source, nothing to hide">
		AccessBay is free and open source under the GPL. You can read every line that runs on your site.
	</Card>

## From paid order to happy customer

<div class="steps">

1. <strong>Add your product.</strong> Create the plugin, theme or software you sell. Set its prices and add each release.
2. <strong>Sell it.</strong> Your customer pays through WooCommerce. Their licence key is created and sent straight away.
3. <strong>Deliver and protect.</strong> Their site activates the key and gets updates. They see their licences, sites and downloads in a portal, without emailing you.

</div>

## Questions before you sell

<details>
<summary>Do I need WooCommerce?</summary>

Today, yes. You take orders through WooCommerce. A checkout built into AccessBay is planned. The [roadmap](/roadmap/) tracks it.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Can I sell through resellers or agencies?</summary>

Not yet. It is planned as a Pro feature. A reseller or agency would buy a licence pool (a block of licences bought once), hand out licences to its own clients and get wholesale pricing. The [roadmap](/roadmap/) tracks it.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Is the free plugin complete?</summary>

Yes. Free covers licences, updates, the customer portal and licence emails. Pro is a planned extra for later features.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Where does my data live?</summary>

On your own WordPress site. Your customers, orders and licences stay with you, and no marketplace sits in between.
</details>

<details>
<summary>What happens on a refund?</summary>

The licence is taken back. When a WooCommerce order is refunded or disputed, AccessBay reverses the licence it created.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Can I put licensing inside my own plugin?</summary>

Yes. The SDK, currently in beta, adds licence checks, a licence screen and updates to your plugin or theme, so buyers never leave it.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Can I connect my own tools?</summary>

Yes. You can connect your own tools, and each one can do only what you allow.
</details>

<details>
<summary>What if my email provider goes down?</summary>

Licence emails switch to another provider, and AccessBay alerts you. Your buyers still get their keys.
</details>

<details>
<summary>How do I install it?</summary>

Follow the [installation guide](/guide/installation/). It also lists what your server needs.
</details>

## Changelog
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/changelog/
Description: What changed in each version of AccessBay and its SDK, newest first.

This page lists what changed in each release of AccessBay and the AccessBay SDK, newest first.

## AccessBay 1.0.0

First public release.

- Licence keys, activations and seats, created from paid WooCommerce orders and reversed on refund or dispute.
- Update delivery for the software you sell, with signed manifests and short-lived download links.
- The AccessBay SDK as a versioned zip.
- Admin screens for the home overview, products and prices, releases, licences, activations, customers, orders, the WooCommerce mapping, the email log, API keys, settings and health.
- Email delivery through `wp_mail` by default, with optional SMTP, Brevo, Resend, Postmark, SMTP2GO, ZeptoMail, Mailgun and SendGrid providers. Failover between providers, and a log of every email and every site-wide `wp_mail` send.
- A test email to any address through one provider, hourly checks of each provider and an optional daily test send. Alerts appear on the AccessBay screens and by email when a provider fails and when it recovers.
- The licence key on the WooCommerce thank-you page and in email, and a customer portal with licences, sites and downloads.
- WP-CLI commands and a REST API with scoped API keys.
- One filter row on the Products, Orders, Licences and Activations screens, with search, filter menus that take several values at once, Clear filters, and saved views in a Views menu. These replace the status tabs. The email log tabs get filters too.
- Search that also finds settings. Open the search dialog with the `/` key, and a result for a field opens its section and puts the cursor in the field.
- The admin has no top bar on larger screens. Search sits under the logo and the theme toggle sits beside the Docs link. A screen inside another shows its parent as a dimmed link in front of the title, as in "Products > Add product".
- Every health check explains its result in plain words. Warnings and critical results come with steps: links to the right admin page, and WP-CLI commands and `wp-config.php` lines you can copy. The Overall card counts and lists what needs attention.
- Yes/no settings are full-width rows, and the "AccessBay in the admin bar" link appears or disappears as soon as you save.
- The email provider picker shows the services as cards with their logos and puts WordPress (`wp_mail`) first, for sites where another SMTP plugin should send. The SendGrid provider is named Twilio SendGrid (API). SMTP2GO accepts an optional bearer token for its webhook.
- The REST list routes that back these screens take several values for one filter, as an array or a comma-separated list. Values in one filter are alternatives, and different filters combine.

## SDK 0.1.0-beta.1

- The first versioned zip of the SDK, released with each AccessBay release. There is no public package registry: unpack the zip and use it through a Composer `path` repository.
- A licence client to activate, deactivate and validate a key against your own AccessBay install. It accepts only answers signed by a public key you pinned.
- An updater: WordPress offers a new version of your plugin from a signed release document, and the SDK checks the package's size and SHA-256 before it is installed.
- A licence screen, a Site Health test, WP-CLI commands and an uninstaller, so a plugin does not need to write them.
- On the licence screen, a "Licence" link on the plugin's row on the Plugins screen, and a "Receive beta updates" switch. A defined `{PREFIX}_CHANNEL` constant still wins and locks the switch.
- The licence screen's title is your `page_title` message or else the plugin's own name.

New versions are added here as they are released.

## Extension points
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/developers/extension-points/
Description: How other plugins can extend AccessBay, today and later.

AccessBay has no public extension points for third-party plugins yet. The only plugin that extends it is AccessBay Pro,
which uses the surface listed [below](#accessbay-pro).

Internally, AccessBay is built from modules that add their own REST routes, settings, health checks and background
jobs through shared contracts. Those contracts are not a public API: they can change in any release, and a third-party
plugin that uses them may break on update.

Today, integrate through the [REST API](/developers/rest-conventions/), which is versioned (`accessbay/v1`) and
documented route by route in the [API reference](/api/). Public extension points, with the same care for
compatibility, are coming in a later release and will be listed here.

## AccessBay Pro

AccessBay Pro is the one plugin that reaches into AccessBay (Free) today, through the surface below. This section is
the contract between the two.

### Version handshake

- Pro declares the oldest Free it works with (`REQUIRES_FREE` in `accessbay-pro.php`) and compares it with the
  **public constant `AccessBay\PLUGIN_VERSION`**, which Free defines when its main file loads and keeps defined.
- When Free is missing or older than that, Pro stands down. It registers no hook, adds nothing to Free, shows an admin
  notice and never fatals. Pro registers all its hooks from one gate on `plugins_loaded` priority 0, so a hook added
  later inherits the stand-down.
- The check is one-directional. Pro checks Free; Free does not check Pro. Free keeps a public item for one minor
  version after deprecating it, which is what lets an older Pro keep working. The first time Free removes a public item
  that a released Pro uses, add a minimum-Pro check in Free or a maximum-Free check in Pro.
- The Free/Pro version matrix suite (`47-pro-matrix.sh`) simulates upgrading in either order with a copy of Pro that
  needs a newer Free. It does not perform a real plugin update.

### Free names Pro may use

Anything else in AccessBay is internal. Pro's tests fail on a `AccessBay\` name that is not listed here, so adding a
name is a reviewed change to this list.

- `AccessBay\PLUGIN_VERSION` — the version handshake above.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Application\Database\Connection` — the database connection a migration runs on.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Application\Migrations\Migration` — a numbered migration.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Application\Migrations\MigrationSet` — one plugin's migrations under its own slug.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Application\Migrations\Step` — one step of a migration.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Application\Migrations\DdlStep` — a step that runs table DDL.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Application\Migrations\CreateTable` — a table definition.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Application\Migrations\AlterTable` — a step that adds a column when it is missing.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Infrastructure\Migrations\InnoDbTables` — the shared check that a migration's tables exist and are
  InnoDB. It lives under `Infrastructure` for now; it moves to `Platform\Application\Migrations` in a later release.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Presentation\Admin\PluginActionLinks` — the "Manage" link on a plugin's row.
- `AccessBay\Plugin` — only the scaffold marker constant; removed with Pro's placeholder class.
- `AccessBay\Licensing\Application\Activations` — the activation counts per plugin version, for Pro's versions report.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Presentation\Rest\AddOnRoutes` — the add-on route manifest an add-on returns from `accessbay/rest/add_ons`.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Presentation\Rest\AddOnRoute` — one route in that manifest.
- `AccessBay\Platform\Presentation\Rest\HttpMethod` — the method of an add-on route.

### Free hook Pro uses

- `accessbay/platform/migration_sets` (filter) — Pro appends its `MigrationSet`. Free reads the filter in its
  `plugins_loaded` priority 1 schema upgrade, so a plugin must register its callback by priority 0.
- `accessbay/delivery/release_channels` (filter) — Pro adds the `beta` channel (`latest-beta.json`).
- `accessbay/rest/add_ons` (filter) — Pro adds its routes' manifest (`/pro/...`, operation ids `pro*`).

## Hooks
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/developers/hooks/
Description: AccessBay's public actions and filters.

AccessBay has **no public hooks yet**.

The plugin does register WordPress actions and filters for its own use, and you may find their names in the code.
They are internal: they can change or disappear in any release without notice, so don't build on them.

A reference of public actions and filters, each with its arguments and the release it arrived in, is coming in a
later release. Until then, the [REST API](/developers/rest-conventions/) is the supported way to integrate.

## Network calls
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/developers/network-calls/
Description: Every request AccessBay and the AccessBay SDK make over the network, when they make it, and what each one sends.

**AccessBay and the SDK send no telemetry.** They send no usage statistics, analytics or crash reports to anyone, and
nothing is sent to any server run by the people who built AccessBay. This page lists every HTTP request the code
makes in this release, so you can check that for yourself and copy the list into your own privacy text.

There are six kinds of request:

| Who sends it | Where it goes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| The SDK inside a vendor's plugin | The vendor's own AccessBay install, at the `server_url` the vendor configured | Activate, check and deactivate a licence, and ask for an update package |
| The SDK's updater inside a vendor's plugin | The host in the plugin's `Update URI` header (or the `meta_url` the vendor configured), and the address the install returns for a package | Read the release information and download an update |
| The AccessBay plugin | The same WordPress site it runs on | Health checks |
| Action Scheduler, a library bundled in the AccessBay plugin | The same WordPress site it runs on | Start the background job runner |
| The AccessBay plugin | `www.cloudflare.com`, only when an administrator runs a command | Refresh the list of Cloudflare's address ranges |
| The AccessBay plugin | The email provider an administrator added under Settings, Email providers | Send email, check the provider's credentials, send test emails |

Before the AccessBay plugin sends a health check, an email provider request or the Cloudflare request, it looks the host name up through your
server's DNS resolver. Those names are the site's own name, `www.cloudflare.com` and the provider hosts you chose, and your resolver sees them.

The updater's requests are listed in their own section near the end.

## The SDK's calls to your AccessBay install

The SDK is a library a vendor builds into a plugin. These calls come from the licence client in that plugin, to the
address its vendor configured as `server_url`. If the plugin isn't configured correctly, the client is `unconfigured`
and makes no call at all.

Every call in this section is a `POST` with a JSON body to `{server_url}/?rest_route=/accessbay/v1/{route}`. This form works on every
permalink setting. The licence key and the activation token travel in the body or in a header and never in the URL.

Every call sends these headers: `Accept: application/json`, `Content-Type: application/json` and
`User-Agent: {product}; accessbay-sdk/{sdk version}`, where `{product}` is the vendor's product slug. A call waits up
to 10 seconds for an answer (15 at most), follows no redirect and reads at most 1 MiB. The SDK never turns off
certificate checks.

| Call | Route | Fields sent in the body | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| Activate | `licenses/activate` | `license_key`, `product`, `site_url`, `environment`, `plugin_version`, `nonce` | When someone presses **Activate** on the licence screen, runs `wp your-command license activate`, or the vendor's code calls `activate()` |
| Validate | `licenses/validate` | `license_key`, `product`, `site_url`, `plugin_version`, `nonce` | About once a day after a key is stored, when someone runs `wp your-command license recheck`, or when the vendor's code calls `validate()` |
| Deactivate | `activations/deactivate` | `activation_token` | When someone presses **Deactivate**, runs `wp your-command license deactivate`, or deletes the plugin and its `uninstall.php` calls the SDK's `Uninstaller` (this one waits 5 seconds at most) |

What the fields hold:

- `license_key`: the licence key the site owner entered.
- `product`: the vendor's product slug.
- `site_url`: the site's home URL, from WordPress's `home_url()`.
- `environment`: the site's WordPress environment type: `local`, `development`, `staging` or `production`. It is a
  hint, and the server decides for itself whether a site is staging. Activate only.
- `plugin_version`: the `Version` header of your plugin, such as `1.4.2` or `2.0.0-beta.1`. The vendor's install stores
  the last one each activation reported, so the vendor can see which versions run in the wild. It is left out when
  the header is not a plain version string (digits and dots, with an optional `-tag`, at most 32 characters).
- `nonce`: 24 random bytes, written in base64url, made fresh for every request and kept in memory until the answer
  arrives. The server signs it into its answer, which is how the SDK knows the answer belongs to that request.
- `activation_token`: the token the server handed out when the site was activated.

The signed answer carries `expires_at`: the licence's own end as a positive integer in unix seconds, or `null` for a
licence with no expiry. The SDK refuses an answer whose `expires_at` is zero or negative. Servers older than this field
leave it out.

The daily check is a WordPress scheduled event planned for 24 hours after the last one plus a random 0 to 2 hours. It
is planned once a key is stored, and deactivating the plugin removes it. A validate that repeats within 60 seconds of
a good one is answered from the stored result and sends nothing. After a failed validate, the daily check waits
before it tries again, 5 minutes at first and growing to 6 hours, plus up to 20% random extra on each wait but never
more than 6 hours in all. If the server sends a `Retry-After` header, the wait is that long instead, capped at 6 hours,
with no extra. Nothing is sent while it waits, unless someone forces a check with `recheck`.

The SDK doesn't call the server's heartbeat route and sends nothing else: no list of plugins, no WordPress or PHP
version, no user names or email addresses.

## The AccessBay plugin's health checks

AccessBay checks its own setup with requests to **the site it runs on**. These requests reach only the site's own
scheme, host and port, follow no redirect, wait 5 seconds at most and read at most 64 KB. They go through the site's
public address, so a cache or CDN in front of the site sees them, which is what the checks look for. The cache check
doesn't send its requests when the site's name points at a private address, and reports the result as unverified.

| Check | Request | Sent |
|---|---|---|
| Cache in front of the site | Two `GET` requests, 2 seconds apart, to the site's `accessbay/v1/health/cache-canary` route | The headers `Accept: application/json` and `User-Agent: AccessBay`. No body. |
| File storage not reachable from the web | One `GET` to the same canary route, then, after AccessBay writes a short-lived test file into its storage directory, one `GET` for each public address that file could be served from. AccessBay deletes the file afterwards. | The same headers. No body. |

Each check is due once a day. A due check runs at the end of an administrator's request, a WP-Cron request or a WP-CLI
command, or after a visitor's response has already gone out. `wp accessbay health` runs every check now.

## The background job runner

AccessBay runs its recurring jobs through Action Scheduler, a library that ships inside the plugin. When anyone
loads a WordPress admin page, or the site receives an `admin-ajax.php` request, and a job is due, Action Scheduler
starts its queue runner with one request, at most once a minute. The request is a `POST`, sent without waiting for an answer, to **your own site's**
`admin-ajax.php`. It carries the action name `as_async_request_queue_runner`, a WordPress nonce and the cookies of the
request that triggered it, including that user's login cookies if they are logged in. Action Scheduler doesn't check the
certificate on this request by default. It carries no licence key or other licence data, and it never leaves your site.

## The Cloudflare address ranges

AccessBay ships with a list of Cloudflare's address ranges. It never refreshes the list by itself. When an
administrator runs `wp accessbay proxies refresh`, it sends two `GET` requests: `https://www.cloudflare.com/ips-v4` and
`https://www.cloudflare.com/ips-v6`. Each carries the header `User-Agent: AccessBay` and nothing from your site.
Cloudflare sees the address of your server, as any web server would. AccessBay keeps the previous list if an answer is
empty or malformed.

## Email provider requests

By default AccessBay sends its email through WordPress's own `wp_mail()` and makes no request of its own for it. The
requests below happen only after an administrator adds a provider under AccessBay > Settings > Email providers
([Email setup](/guide/email/)). Each goes to the host of that provider and nowhere else. The API providers are reached over HTTPS only.

| Provider | Hosts |
|---|---|
| Brevo | `api.brevo.com` |
| Resend | `api.resend.com` |
| Postmark | `api.postmarkapp.com` |
| SMTP2GO | `api.smtp2go.com`, or `us-api.smtp2go.com`, `eu-api.smtp2go.com`, `au-api.smtp2go.com` |
| ZeptoMail | `cpaas.zoho.com` by default, or `cpaas.zoho.eu`, `api.zeptomail.com`, `api.zeptomail.eu` |
| Mailgun | `api.mailgun.net`, or `api.eu.mailgun.net` |
| Twilio SendGrid | `api.sendgrid.com`, or `api.eu.sendgrid.com` |
| SMTP | The mail server host and port the administrator typed in |

AccessBay makes these requests:

- **Sending an email.** One request per attempt, when AccessBay sends an email through that provider. It carries the
  recipient, sender, subject and body of that email, and the provider's key or login.
- **Test connection.** A check of the key or login. ZeptoMail and SMTP2GO can't check without sending, so for them it
  sends a short test email to the administrator's own address.
- **Hourly credential check.** Once an hour for each enabled provider that can check its credentials without sending.
  Providers that can't are judged from their real sends.
- **Send test email.** One short email to an address the administrator types, through the provider they pick.
- **Daily test email.** Only if the administrator turned on **Send a daily test email**. One short email through each
  provider once a day.

Webhooks come in, not out: a provider calls your site's webhook URL to report what happened to an email, and AccessBay
sends nothing back. A provider's host only learns what an email carries and the address of your server.

## Not network calls of AccessBay

- **Email through `wp_mail`.** The default provider, WordPress (`wp_mail`), hands the message to WordPress's own
  `wp_mail()`, so whichever SMTP or mail service your site is set up to use carries it. What that service receives is
  between your site and that service.
- **WordPress itself.** Requests made by WordPress core or by other plugins, such as update checks for WordPress and
  for plugins hosted on WordPress.org, aren't made by AccessBay or the SDK.

## The SDK's updater

The updater is part of the SDK. It hooks WordPress's own plugin update check for the host in the plugin's `Update URI`
header, so it has no timer of its own: the first two calls below happen inside WordPress's update check (twice a day,
and when someone opens the Plugins screen), and the rest when an update is installed, by hand or automatically. If the
site disallows file changes (`DISALLOW_FILE_MODS`), the install steps send nothing.

| Call | Where | Sent | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read the release information | `GET {meta_url}{product}/latest.json`. `meta_url` defaults to `https://{host of the plugin's Update URI}/meta/`. | No key, no site URL and no body. When the site's owner opted in to beta (see [Release channels](#release-channels)) the file is `latest-beta.json`. The headers `Accept: application/json` and `User-Agent: {product}; accessbay-sdk/{sdk version}`. It waits 10 seconds at most, follows no redirect and reads at most 64 KiB. | Inside the update check, unless a failed read (no answer, a 429 or a 5xx) is still being waited out |
| Check the licence first | The Validate call above | As above | Before that read, if the last verified answer is more than 12 hours old and the SDK isn't waiting after a failure |
| Ask for the package | `POST {server_url}/?rest_route=/accessbay/v1/packages` on your AccessBay install | The header `X-AccessBay-Activation` with the activation token, and the same `Accept`, `Content-Type` and `User-Agent` headers as the other calls. No body, except `{"channel":"beta"}` when the site's owner opted in to beta. It waits 10 seconds at most and follows no redirect. | When an update is installed, and only if the licence allows updates |
| Activate again, then ask once more | The Activate call above, then the previous call again | As above | Only when the server answers 403 to the token while the site believes it is activated, which is what a token replaced by a second activation looks like. At most once per install attempt. |
| Download the package | The address your install returns, which must be `https` (plain `http` only for a local host when the site's environment type is `local` or `development`) | A plain `GET` made with WordPress's safe HTTP client. It sends only the header `User-Agent: {product}; accessbay-sdk/{sdk version}`, not WordPress's default one, so no site URL goes to the package host. It stops reading after the signed size plus one byte and waits 5 minutes at most. The host may differ from your install, such as file storage. | Straight after the package request |

The update row WordPress shows carries only a placeholder for the package, the address of the SDK's own `packages`
route. It is never fetched. The SDK swaps it for the real, one-use address when the install starts, because that address
expires after 60 seconds.

The SDK checks the downloaded file against a signed SHA-256 and size before WordPress unpacks it, and discards it on any
mismatch. When the licence has lapsed, the update still shows but the package request and the download don't happen,
and automatic updates for that plugin stop.

### Release channels

A site gets stable releases unless its owner opts in to beta. The owner sets the constant `{PREFIX}_CHANNEL` to `beta`
(in `wp-config.php`), or the option `{prefix}_channel` to `beta`, where the prefix is the copy's `abs_…` prefix. The
constant wins over the option, and any other value means stable. Opted in, the SDK reads `latest-beta.json` instead of
`latest.json` (the channel is the document's name, not a query value) and adds `{"channel":"beta"}` to the package
request. Your AccessBay install answers with a beta release only when it offers the beta channel
(an add-on such as AccessBay Pro must add it through the `accessbay/delivery/release_channels` filter) and the product
has a live beta release; a request for `latest.json`, or any request sent to an install that does not offer beta,
always gets the newest stable release. A site on beta is also offered a stable release that is newer than the newest beta.

## Check it yourself

In this release, the SDK sends its requests from one file, `src/Http.php`: the licence calls and the package request
through `wp_remote_post()`, the release information through `wp_remote_get()` and the package download through
`wp_safe_remote_get()`. In the AccessBay plugin's own code, the one class that sends a request is
`WpPinnedTransport`, behind `SafeHttpClient`, and the email provider drivers use it. The SMTP provider connects to its
mail server through PHPMailer instead. A search for `wp_remote_` and `wp_safe_remote_` in the SDK's `src/` folder and
the plugin's `src/` folder finds those two places. The bundled job runner sends
one more request. To find it, search `vendor-prefixed/woocommerce/action-scheduler` for `wp_remote_post`.

## REST conventions
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/developers/rest-conventions/
Description: The rules every AccessBay REST route follows, including authentication, errors, retries, rate limits and headers.

## Namespace

Every route lives under `accessbay/v1`:

```text
https://example.com/wp-json/accessbay/v1/…
```

With plain permalinks, use `https://example.com/?rest_route=/accessbay/v1/…`. The [API reference](/api/) lists every
route with its parameters and answers, generated from the same route registry the plugin uses.

## Who may call a route

Each route is one of three kinds.

| Kind | Who | How it authenticates |
|---|---|---|
| Admin | A logged-in WordPress user with the route's capability | The login cookie plus a `wp_rest` nonce in the `X-WP-Nonce` header, on every method |
| Public | Anyone | Nothing; rate limited |
| API | Machines, such as your own servers | Scoped API keys: coming in a later release. No API route exists yet |

For admin routes:

- Without a nonce, WordPress treats the request as anonymous: `401 accessbay_unauthenticated`.
- A nonce in the `_wpnonce` query parameter doesn't count: `403 accessbay_invalid_nonce`.
- Application Passwords are refused: `403 accessbay_application_password_refused`.
- A user without the route's capability gets `403 accessbay_forbidden`.

## Errors

Errors use WordPress's shape:

```json
{
  "code": "accessbay_rate_limited",
  "message": "Too many requests. Wait and try again.",
  "data": { "status": 429 }
}
```

Match on `code`, never on `message`, which is translated. Codes are AccessBay's own (below) or WordPress core's,
such as `rest_invalid_param`, `rest_no_route` and `rest_cookie_invalid_nonce`. Parameters are validated before
authorisation, so an invalid parameter answers `400 rest_invalid_param` even to a caller who may not use the route.

| Code | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `accessbay_credential_in_url` | 400 | A credential (`key`, `license_key`, `token`, `api_key`) was sent in the query string |
| `accessbay_envelope_refused` | 400 | `?_envelope=` is not supported |
| `accessbay_method_override_refused` | 400 | `?_method=` and `X-HTTP-Method-Override` are not supported |
| `accessbay_unauthenticated` | 401 | No logged-in user |
| `accessbay_api_key_invalid` | 401 | The API key is missing or not valid |
| `accessbay_application_password_refused` | 403 | Application Passwords can't call AccessBay routes |
| `accessbay_invalid_nonce` | 403 | The `X-WP-Nonce` header is missing or not valid |
| `accessbay_forbidden` | 403 | The user lacks the route's capability |
| `accessbay_method_not_allowed` | 405 | The path exists but not with this method; the `Allow` header lists the methods it takes |
| `accessbay_rate_limited` | 429 | Too many requests; wait for the seconds in `Retry-After` |
| `accessbay_internal_error` | 500 | An unexpected failure; it is logged on the site |
| `accessbay_temporarily_unavailable` | 503 | Something AccessBay depends on is unavailable; try again later |

## Retrying

`503 accessbay_temporarily_unavailable` always means "try again later". It never means a key, licence or request is
invalid, so a client must not act on it as if it did (for example, by deactivating a licence). AccessBay answers it
when a health check has switched a feature off, when the site secret is missing in live mode or can't be read, and when
the rate limiter can't count. When the answer has a `Retry-After` header, wait that many seconds before retrying;
otherwise back off.

## Rate limits

Public routes are limited per client address and across the whole site (the health ping, for example, takes 60
requests a minute per client and 6000 a minute in total). Over a limit, the answer is `429 accessbay_rate_limited`
with `Retry-After` in seconds.

Limits count per client address. Behind a reverse proxy or CDN, AccessBay reads forwarding headers only from proxies you
trust (the `trusted_proxies` and `cloudflare_proxies` settings). Until you set them, every visitor arriving through the
proxy shares the proxy's address.

## Methods

- A path that exists but doesn't take the method answers `405` with an `Allow` header.
- `HEAD` works wherever `GET` does.
- Batch requests (`/batch/v1`) are refused for every AccessBay route.

## Headers

Every answer, errors included, sends `Cache-Control: no-store, private` and `Vary: Cookie`, and no
`Access-Control-*` headers: no AccessBay route is meant to be called from a browser on another site. JSONP is off.

## Filtering list routes

The admin screens that list things (products, orders, licences, activations, the email log and the site mail log)
read their rows from list routes. These routes take a `POST` with a JSON body, like every admin route (see "Who may
call a route" above). All body fields are optional.

| Route | Filters that take several values | Other body fields |
|---|---|---|
| `/accessbay/v1/products/list` | `status`: `draft`, `active`, `archived` | `before_id`, `limit` |
| `/accessbay/v1/orders/search` | `source`: `woocommerce`, `native`, `manual`, `api`; `payment_status`: `pending`, `paid`, `partially_refunded`, `refunded`, `charged_back`, `cancelled`; `fulfilment_status`: `unfulfilled`, `partially_fulfilled`, `fulfilled`, `partially_revoked`, `revoked`, `not_required` | `q` (up to 191 characters), `page`, `limit` |
| `/accessbay/v1/licenses/search` | `status`: `unstarted`, `active`, `expired`, `void`, `suspended`, `revoked`; `mode`: `test`, `live`; `key_origin`: `generated`, `imported` | `product_id`, `customer_id`, `license_key`, `before_id`, `limit` |
| `/accessbay/v1/activations/search` | `state`: `live`, `deactivated` | `staging` (true or false), `page`, `limit` |
| `/accessbay/v1/admin/outbox/list` | `status`: `queued`, `held`, `accepted`, `suppressed`, `failed`, `cancelled`, `bounced`; `delivery`: `deferred`, `delivered`, `bounced`, `complained` | `provider_id`, `before_id`, `limit` |
| `/accessbay/v1/admin/mail/site-log` | `result`: `sent`, `failed` | `recipient` (up to 190 characters), `before_id`, `limit` |

`limit` is at most 100. The [API reference](/api/) has the full list of fields and answers for each route.

Each filter in the first column accepts one value, a comma-separated string or an array:

```json
{ "status": "active,draft", "limit": 25 }
```

```json
{ "status": ["active", "draft"], "limit": 25 }
```

Both bodies ask for products that are active or draft. The rules:

- Values inside one filter are alternatives (OR). A row matches when it has any of them.
- Different filters combine (AND). This body asks for orders that are paid or partly refunded, and also not yet
  fulfilled:

  ```json
  {
    "payment_status": ["paid", "partially_refunded"],
    "fulfilment_status": "unfulfilled"
  }
  ```

- A single value works as it always did. An empty string, an empty array or `null` means no filter.
- Spaces around a value are removed and a repeated value counts once.
- An unknown value answers `400 rest_invalid_param`, so a typo never turns into "no filter" silently.
- A list longer than the number of allowed values is refused.

## SDK
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/developers/sdk/
Description: Add AccessBay licensing to your own WordPress plugin with the SDK. Install it, prefix it, configure it, test it and release it.

The AccessBay SDK is a small PHP library you build into a WordPress plugin you sell. It activates a licence key
against your own AccessBay install, checks that every answer is signed by that install, and tells your plugin whether
the licence is active. It also supplies a licence screen, WP-CLI commands and a Site Health test, so you write none of
them.

**Status.** The licence client described here is built. Update delivery, where WordPress offers your customers a new
version and the SDK checks its signature and SHA-256 before installing it, **lands with the updater** and isn't in the
SDK yet. Sections that depend on it say so.

The SDK never talks to anyone but the AccessBay install you configure. The [network calls](/developers/network-calls/)
page lists every request it makes and every field it sends.

## Requirements

- PHP 7.4 or newer on the sites that run your plugin. The SDK uses no newer syntax.
- An AccessBay install of your own, reachable over `https`, with your product set up on it. Its address is your
  `server_url`, and the product's slug is your `product`.
- To build your plugin: Composer, PHP 8.1 or newer (Strauss needs it), and a network connection for Composer. The
  finished plugin still runs on PHP 7.4.

## Install with Composer

AccessBay has no public package registry, so you don't install the SDK with `composer require` from Packagist. Each
AccessBay release ships the SDK as a versioned zip beside the plugin zips: `accessbay-sdk-<version>.zip` and its
`.sha256` file. Check it with `sha256sum -c accessbay-sdk-<version>.zip.sha256`, then unpack it next to your plugin's
`composer.json`. You get one folder, `accessbay-sdk/`, holding `src/`, `composer.json`, `LICENSE`, `README.md`,
`CHANGELOG.md` and `example-plugin/`. Point a Composer `path` repository at that folder. The package name inside it is
`wpanchorbay/accessbay-sdk`, and its version (in `composer.json` and the newest `CHANGELOG.md` heading) is the SDK's
own, not the AccessBay plugin's. The example plugin in `example-plugin/` does the same, and so does the sample below.
Keep `accessbay-sdk/` out of your own release zip: your plugin ships only the copy Strauss prefixes. The
constraint `^0.1@beta` takes fixes within 0.1 and never a breaking 0.2 or 1.0; raise it when you move up.

## Prefix it with Strauss

Never ship the SDK under its own namespace. If two plugins on one site both did, PHP would load one copy for both. The
SDK would then refuse to run (see [Two vendors on one site](#two-vendors-on-one-site)). Strauss copies the SDK and its
one dependency, `paragonie/sodium_compat`, into a folder and renames their namespaces and classes to a prefix you choose.

Choose three prefixes that belong to you: a namespace, a class prefix and a constant prefix. This `composer.json` is the
example plugin's with a different vendor name:

```json
{
  "name": "acme/acme-pro",
  "type": "wordpress-plugin",
  "license": "GPL-2.0-or-later",
  "repositories": [ { "type": "path", "url": "./accessbay-sdk", "options": { "symlink": false } } ],
  "require": {
    "php": ">=7.4",
    "wpanchorbay/accessbay-sdk": "^0.1@beta"
  },
  "require-dev": { "brianhenryie/strauss": "0.30.*" },
  "config": { "sort-packages": true },
  "extra": {
    "strauss": {
      "target_directory": "vendor-prefixed",
      "namespace_prefix": "Acme\\Vendor\\",
      "classmap_prefix": "Acme_Vendor_",
      "constant_prefix": "ACME_VENDOR_",
      "delete_vendor_packages": true,
      "override_autoload": { "paragonie/sodium_compat": { "classmap": [ "src/" ] } },
      "exclude_from_copy": { "file_patterns": [ "#paragonie/sodium_compat/(lib|namespaced)/#", "#paragonie/sodium_compat/autoload#" ] }
    }
  }
}
```

Keep the `override_autoload` and `exclude_from_copy` lines. With Strauss's defaults, some of `sodium_compat`'s global
classes stay unprefixed.

Build it:

```sh
composer install
vendor/bin/strauss
```

Strauss's own autoloader doesn't list every class it writes. The example plugin therefore replaces it with a classmap
of the whole `vendor-prefixed/` folder. Run this in the folder that will become your plugin, after copying
`vendor-prefixed/` into it from the build folder:

```sh
rm -rf vendor-prefixed/autoload.php vendor-prefixed/composer
printf '{ "autoload": { "classmap": [ "vendor-prefixed/" ] } }\n' > composer.json
composer dump-autoload --classmap-authoritative
rm composer.json
```

That produces `vendor/autoload.php`, which your main plugin file requires. `example-plugin/build.sh` does all of this
and zips the result; copy it as the start of your own release script.

## Start the client and set the config

Call `Client::boot()` while your main plugin file loads, never on the `init` hook. This is the example plugin's whole
integration, with the Strauss namespace from above:

```php
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Acme Pro
 * Version: 1.0.0
 * Requires PHP: 7.4
 * Update URI: https://updates.example.com/acme-pro/
 */

defined( 'ABSPATH' ) || exit;

require_once __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

$acme_client = \Acme\Vendor\AccessBay\Sdk\Client::boot(
	array(
		'server_url'  => 'https://licences.example.com',
		'product'     => 'acme-pro',
		'public_keys' => array( 'your-kid' => 'base64 public key from your AccessBay install' ),
		'plugin_file' => __FILE__,
	)
);
```

Pass `server_url`, `product` and `public_keys` as a literal array, as above. Don't pass them through a filter: a filter
would let any snippet on the site swap your licence server or your signing keys.

`boot()` registers hooks and reads no option and runs no query on a front-end request. Calling it again for the same
plugin folder returns the first client.

| Key | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `server_url` | yes | The origin of your AccessBay install, such as `https://licences.example.com`. It must start with `https://`. `http://` is accepted only for a local server (loopback or private address) when the site's environment type is `local` or `development`. |
| `product` | yes | Your product's slug on the install: lower-case letters, digits, `_`, `.` and `-`, starting with a letter or digit, at most 64 characters. |
| `public_keys` | yes | A map of key id to the base64 Ed25519 public key. See [The public key](#the-public-key). |
| `plugin_file` | yes | The absolute path of your main plugin file. `__FILE__` in that file is right. |
| `cli_command` | no | The WP-CLI command name. Defaults to the product slug. |
| `admin_page` | no | `true` (the default) shows the SDK's licence screen. `false` hides it so you can build your own on the client's methods. |
| `offline_grace_days` | no | Whole days from 1 to 30, default 7. How long the plugin keeps a licence usable when the server can't be reached. It can only shorten the deadline the server signed, never lengthen it. |
| `messages` | no | Your own wording for the SDK's screen texts, as a map of message id to text, for example `'page_title' => 'Acme Pro licence'`. |
| `mode` | no | `live` (the default), or `test` when `server_url` is a sandbox install. A live client refuses a test licence's answer, and the reverse. |
| `meta_url` | no | Lands with the updater. Not read yet. |

**A bad config sends nothing.** If a required value is missing or malformed, `server_url` isn't `https`, the plugin
file can't be read, or a public key isn't 32 bytes once decoded, `boot()` returns a client with the status
`unconfigured`. That client makes no network request, every method returns a failed result naming the key at fault, and
administrators see an error notice on the Plugins screen. Each request that boots it writes one line to the PHP error
log. In a `local` or `development` environment with `WP_DEBUG` on, `boot()` throws a `ConfigException` instead, so you
can't miss the mistake. It never throws on `staging` or `production`: a notice is a smaller problem for your customers
than a blank screen.

## Update URI

Put an `Update URI` header on your main plugin file, with an `https` address on a domain you control, as the example
does. WordPress uses the header's host to choose which filter offers updates for the plugin, and the updater uses the
same host as the default place to read the public release information, unless you set `meta_url`. **This lands with the
updater.** The licence client in this release doesn't read the header, so nothing happens yet when you add it.

## The public key

Your AccessBay install signs every answer. The SDK accepts an answer only if it verifies against a key you pinned in
your plugin, and it never fetches a key.

On the AccessBay install, run:

```sh
wp accessbay keys show
```

Among the lines it prints is `Signing key:` followed by JSON holding `kid`, `alg` and `pk`. Put `kid` and `pk` into
`public_keys` as `array( 'kid' => 'pk' )`. An answer signed with a key id that isn't in your map is refused.

The map can hold more than one entry. To rotate a key without a gap, ship a release that carries both the current
and the next key before your install starts signing with the next one.

## Use the licence in your plugin

`boot()` returns the client. Keep it where the rest of your plugin can reach it.

```php
$acme_client->status()->code;            // active, grace, lapsed, inactive, invalid or unconfigured
$acme_client->entitled( 'acme-pro' );    // true when the signed entitlements include this slug
$acme_client->updates_allowed();         // true only when the status is active or grace
$acme_client->masked_key();              // the stored key with only its last four characters visible

$acme_client->on_status_change(
	function ( $current, $previous ) {
		// Called whenever the status code changes. Both arguments are Status objects.
	}
);
```

`status()` also gives you `reason` (for display only), `checked_at`, `access_until`, `grace_until`, `expires_at` (the licence's own end in unix seconds, `0` for no expiry), `entitlements` and
`staging`. `activate( $key )`, `deactivate()` and `validate()` each return an `Outcome` with `ok`, `status`, `code`,
`message`, `retry_after` and `server_code`. A refused key, a full licence or a network failure comes back as an
`Outcome` and never throws.

Gate features on `entitled()`, not on `status()`. A lapsed licence stops updates and support, not features the customer
already bought. `entitled()` stays true through `active`, `grace`, `lapsed` and any network failure. It turns false
only when your install reports the licence revoked, held or void, or when the site never had a verified activation.
To switch features off when your install reports a licence revoked, held or void, check for `status()->code === 'invalid'`.

Only signed fields decide the status. The status, seat counts and messages in the server's answer that aren't signed
are shown to the user and never grant access.

## The licence screen

With `admin_page` left on, the SDK adds one page under **Settings**. By default it is named **Licence (your-product-slug)**. It has:

- the licence **Status** and, once activated, **Expires** (a date, or "No expiry"); Site Health adds **Verified until**;
- the key, shown masked, with **Reveal key**, **Activate** and **Deactivate** buttons;
- a note, **Staging site: this activation does not use a seat.**, when your install counted the site as staging.

Only users who can manage options see it, and every action checks a nonce first. A row under your plugin on the Plugins
screen links to the page whenever the licence isn't active. The SDK adds no top-level menu, dashboard widget or
redirect. Its notices appear on the Plugins screen and on its own page, and nowhere else.

The SDK also registers, for each copy:

- WP-CLI: `wp your-command license status`, `activate <key>`, `deactivate` and `recheck`. Use `activate -` to read the
  key from standard input, because a key given as an argument shows in the process list. `recheck` forces a licence
  check now. A command that fails exits with status 1 and prints the result code, never the key. `your-command` is your
  `cli_command`.
- A Site Health test that reports the licence status and expiry, and a debug section. Neither shows the key.
- A daily check of the licence that is planned once a key is stored.

Translate the SDK's texts in your own text domain, using the `messages` key. The SDK can't use yours.

### Uninstall

Deactivating your plugin stops the daily check and keeps the key. To clean up when the plugin is deleted, call the
SDK from your `uninstall.php` with the same config:

```php
<?php
defined( 'WP_UNINSTALL_PLUGIN' ) || exit;

require_once __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

\Acme\Vendor\AccessBay\Sdk\Uninstaller::run(
	array(
		'server_url'  => 'https://licences.example.com',
		'product'     => 'acme-pro',
		'public_keys' => array( 'your-kid' => 'base64 public key from your AccessBay install' ),
		'plugin_file' => __DIR__ . '/acme-pro.php',
	)
);
```

`Uninstaller::run()` asks your install to free the site's seat (waiting at most 5 seconds, and carrying on if it
can't), deletes the SDK's options and the daily check, and never blocks the uninstall. Don't also register an uninstall
hook for the SDK.

## Two vendors on one site

A site can run plugins from several vendors, each with its own copy of the SDK. Two things keep the copies apart.

**Your prefix.** Strauss gives your copy its own namespace, class prefix and constant prefix, so `Acme\Vendor\...` and
another vendor's `Zeta\Vendor\...` are different classes to PHP. The SDK defines no global function, constant or class
of its own. The one name Strauss doesn't change is the global `SodiumException` class, which both copies share and which
holds no state.

**Names from the plugin folder.** Everything the SDK registers with WordPress is named from the folder your plugin
lives in, not from your product. The prefix `{p}` is `abs_` followed by the folder name with every run of characters
other than letters and digits turned into `_`, in lower case. When that changed the folder name, a short hash of the
original name follows, so `a-b` and `a_b` stay apart. Two plugins can't share a folder on one site, so two copies never
share a name, whatever `product` each configures.

| What | Name |
|---|---|
| Stored key | option `{p}_key` |
| Licence state | option `{p}_state` |
| Update cache | option `{p}_meta` |
| Request lock | option `{p}_lock` |
| Daily check | scheduled event `{p}_recheck` |
| Licence page | `{p}-license` |
| Site Health test | `{p}_license` |
| WP-CLI | `wp {cli_command} license`, left alone with a warning if another copy already registered that name |

The SDK stores no transients and no table, and its options aren't autoloaded.

An unprefixed copy is caught, not trusted. If the SDK's code didn't come from your own plugin folder, because PHP's
autoloader served another plugin's copy, the client turns `unconfigured` and tells the administrator to prefix the SDK.

**Renaming your plugin folder changes `{p}`.** The renamed copy starts with no key and no state, so your customers
must enter their key again. A download from GitHub that adds `-main` to the folder name, or a versioned folder name,
does exactly that. Ship the same folder name in every release.

The SDK's tests build the example plugin twice with different prefixes, load both copies in one process, and check that
they share no names and don't touch each other's options.

## Test on a staging site

Do this before every release, on a WordPress site that isn't your customers'.

1. Build the zip with your release script and install it from **Plugins > Add New > Upload Plugin**. Set the site's
   environment type in `wp-config.php`, for example `define( 'WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE', 'staging' );`. The SDK sends the
   environment type with the activation as a hint.
2. Check the Plugins screen. A config error shows as an error notice. If you see one, fix the config key it names and
   stop here.
3. Open **Settings > Licence (your-product-slug)**, paste a test key for your product, and press **Activate**. The
   status should read **Active**, with an **Expires** date, or "No expiry".
4. Run `wp your-command license status`. It prints `status`, `access_until`, `staging` and the masked `key`.
5. Press **Reveal key** and check it shows the key you pasted. Open **Tools > Site Health** and find the licence test:
   it shows the status and expiry and no key.
6. Cut the site's connection to your install, for example with a firewall rule, and run
   `wp your-command license recheck`. It fails with the code `abs_transport`, the status stays as it was, and your
   plugin's `entitled()` checks still pass. Restore the connection and run `recheck` again.
7. Press **Deactivate**. The status returns to **Not activated**.
8. If you run a sandbox install, repeat steps 3 and 4 against it with `'mode' => 'test'`.

Testing on a local server over `http://` works only when the environment type is `local` or `development`.

## Release checklist

Before each release:

- [ ] The release script runs Strauss with your own three prefixes and the `override_autoload` and
  `exclude_from_copy` lines from this guide, and rebuilds the classmap autoloader.
- [ ] No namespace in `vendor-prefixed/` outside your own prefix: `grep -rhE '^namespace ' vendor-prefixed | grep -vF 'Acme\Vendor'` prints nothing (with your prefix in place of `Acme\Vendor`).
- [ ] `server_url`, `product` and `public_keys` are literal values, not read from a filter, a setting or a constant.
- [ ] `public_keys` holds the key id and key that `wp accessbay keys show` prints on your install today.
- [ ] The main plugin file has the `Update URI` header (lands with the updater).
- [ ] The plugin folder in the zip has the same name as in the last release.
- [ ] Your features check `entitled()`, not `status()`, so a lapse or an outage doesn't switch them off.
- [ ] `uninstall.php` calls `Uninstaller::run()` with the same config, and your plugin doesn't also register an
  uninstall hook for the SDK.
- [ ] Your plugin's privacy text lists the calls on the [network calls](/developers/network-calls/) page.
- [ ] The staging test above passed on the zip you are about to ship.
- [ ] The WordPress.org build, if you have one, has no SDK and no updater: no `Update URI` header other than
  WordPress.org's, no `update_plugins_` and no `upgrader_pre_download`. Check it with
  `grep -rnE 'Update URI:|update_plugins_|upgrader_pre_download|plugin-update-checker|PucFactory|AccessBay.*Sdk' <build folder>`,
  which should print nothing.

## Features and use cases
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/features/
Description: Everything AccessBay does today, grouped by what you do with it, and the kinds of software business it fits.

AccessBay turns the WooCommerce store you already have into a licence server for the plugins, themes and software you
sell. This page lists what works in the current release. Anything planned is on the [Roadmap](/roadmap/), not here.

## Features

### Products and releases

- **Products and prices.** Create what you sell as software (a plugin), a digital download or a bundle. Each product
  has prices, and a product stays a draft until you make it active. See [Products](/guide/products/).
- **Releases.** Upload a release, publish it, and pull it back (yank it) if it is bad. The software you sell receives
  a published release as an update.
- **Archiving.** Archiving a product ends new sales. You choose whether customers with a valid licence keep their
  downloads and updates ([Plugin settings](/guide/plugin-settings/)).

### Licensing

- **Licence keys, activations and seats.** A paid order creates a key. The buyer's site activates it, and each licence
  allows a number of sites. See [Licences](/guide/licences/) and [Activations](/guide/activations/).
- **Control from the admin.** Extend a licence by a number of days, add seats, suspend it, revoke it or replace its
  key. Deactivate a site and its seat is free again.
- **Staging sites.** AccessBay can treat a copy of a site as staging, with its own allowance.
- **Test mode.** Keep test orders and licences apart from real ones, and try the licence calls in the API test
  console.

### Orders and checkout through WooCommerce

- **Paid orders create licences.** You map each WooCommerce product to an AccessBay product, and a paid order issues
  the licence on its own.
- **Refunds and disputes reverse access.** A refund on the order ends the licence's access. You record a dispute on
  the order in AccessBay.
- **Orders screen.** See where each order came from, its payment status and whether the buyer received what they
  bought. See [Orders](/guide/orders/).

### Delivery and updates

- **Updates in wp-admin.** Your customers' sites are offered new versions of your plugin or theme in the usual
  WordPress way, from your own site.
- **Signed and short-lived.** Update information is signed, and download links expire.
- **Client SDK (beta).** Add the SDK to your plugin or theme to activate a licence and ask your site for updates. It
  comes as a separate zip with each release, and gives you a licence screen, WP-CLI commands and a Site Health test.
  See [SDK](/developers/sdk/).

### Customers

- **Key on the thank-you page and in email.** The buyer sees the licence key right after paying and gets it by email.
- **Customer portal.** Buyers see their licences and sites, and download the latest or an earlier version of the
  software, without writing to you.
- **Customer list.** See who bought, with email, company and country.

### Email

- **Failover.** Licence emails go through a list of providers you order. If one fails, the next sends the email.
- **Providers.** WordPress mail (`wp_mail`) by default, plus SMTP, Twilio SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Resend, Brevo,
  SMTP2GO and ZeptoMail. See [Email setup](/guide/email/).
- **Log and alerts.** A log of every email, regular checks of each provider, and an alert when one fails and when it
  recovers.

### Admin

- **One place to run it.** Products, orders, licences, activations, customers and the WooCommerce mapping all live
  under AccessBay in wp-admin, with a home screen that lists the next steps.
- **Search and saved views.** Search licences, customers, orders, products and settings from anywhere, and filter and
  save views on every list. See [Search and filters](/guide/finding-things/).
- **Light and dark.** Choose the look in the theme menu.

### REST API and WP-CLI

- **REST API.** Every route is under `accessbay/v1` and listed in the [API reference](/api/). Create API keys with
  limited scopes under AccessBay > API keys, and read [REST conventions](/developers/rest-conventions/).
- **WP-CLI.** `wp accessbay` commands cover products, prices, releases, customers, licences, health and keys, for
  scripts and for setting up a test site.

### Health and security

- **Health checks.** AccessBay checks its own setup (secret, database, background jobs, email, clock, file storage)
  and tells you in plain words how to fix a problem. See [Health checks](/guide/health-checks/).
- **A secret you control.** Stored keys and credentials are encrypted with a secret kept in your server
  configuration. See [The secret key](/guide/secret-key/).
- **No telemetry.** AccessBay and the SDK send no usage data to anyone. [Network calls](/developers/network-calls/)
  lists every request they make.
- **Your data stays.** Deleting the plugin keeps your records unless you opt in to remove them, and you can erase
  everything on purpose from the Settings screen.

### Free and Pro

Everything above is in the free plugin, which works fully on its own. AccessBay Pro is in development and adds no
working features yet, so nothing on this page is Pro only today. The planned Pro features are on the
[Roadmap](/roadmap/).

## Use cases

- **Sell a plugin with a yearly licence.** Create a software product with a price that allows a number of sites for a
  number of days. Buyers get a key, activate it in the plugin, and keep receiving updates while the licence is active.
- **Sell a theme.** The same flow works for a theme. Your theme asks your site for updates through the SDK.
- **Sell a licence for your own software.** Issue a key for each customer. Your software activates and validates it
  against your site through the licence routes in the [API reference](/api/), and the answers are signed.
- **Updates only for paying buyers.** Releases are offered only to sites with a valid licence, and a refund or dispute
  ends access.
- **Limit and manage sites.** Give each licence a number of seats, allow a few staging sites, and deactivate a site
  from the Activations screen when a customer moves.
- **Support a customer.** Look up an order, licence or customer from one search box, extend a licence, add a seat or
  replace a lost key.
- **Keep selling when email breaks.** Add a second provider, and a customer who just paid still sees their key on
  screen and by email.

## What comes next

Renewals, a checkout without WooCommerce, subscriptions and more are planned. See the [Roadmap](/roadmap/) for the
order, and [Known limits](/guide/known-limits/) for what this release leaves out.

## Activations
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/guide/activations/
Description: The Activations screen, what each column means, and how to deactivate a site.

Go to AccessBay > Activations to see the sites that use your licences. A site appears here when a customer enters a
licence key in the plugin. Until then the screen says "No sites have activated yet". Search, filters, saved views and
shareable links are described in [Search and filters](/guide/finding-things/).

## Columns

| Column | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Site | The site's address. A "Staging" tag marks a site AccessBay treats as a staging copy. |
| Licence | A link, "Open licence", to the licence the site uses. |
| Plugin version | The version of the plugin that last reported in. |
| Last seen | When the site last contacted AccessBay, or "Not yet". |
| Status | Live, or Deactivated. |
| Actions | The **Deactivate** button. |

Click **Last seen** or **Site** to sort by it.

## Filters

- **Status:** Live, Deactivated.
- **Staging:** Staging sites, Live sites.

## Deactivate a site

Select **Deactivate** in a row and confirm "Deactivate site". The site stops counting against the licence's site limit
at once. It can activate again with the key.

## Email setup
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/guide/email/
Description: How AccessBay sends email, how to add email providers, what happens when one fails, and what the email logs keep.

AccessBay sends its own emails, such as the licence key after a purchase, through a list of email providers. You
choose the providers and their order. The list starts with one provider, WordPress mail (`wp_mail`), so email works
before you set anything up.

## Start with wp_mail

`wp_mail()` is WordPress's own mail function. AccessBay uses it by default, and it works with any SMTP or
email-service plugin that routes `wp_mail()` through a mail service. If you already have such a plugin, you don't
need to change anything.

AccessBay never replaces `wp_mail()` for the rest of your site. Your other plugins send mail as they did before.

Many hosts deliver mail from PHP poorly or not at all. With `wp_mail` alone, AccessBay can only report that WordPress
accepted an email. It can't say whether the email arrived.

## Why add a second provider

If `wp_mail` is your only provider and it fails, nothing else takes over. A second provider lets AccessBay send the
email another way. The Email providers screen shows an "Add a second email provider" message while `wp_mail` is the
only one, and the "AccessBay email delivery" check in Site Health warns about the same thing.

A customer who buys a licence still sees the licence key and download links on screen after the purchase, so a
failing provider doesn't leave them stuck.

## Add a provider

1. Go to AccessBay > Settings > Email providers.
2. Select **Add provider**.
3. Pick the service you will send through, then select **Continue**. The services show as cards in two columns, each
   with its logo. **WordPress (wp_mail)** comes first, across the full width. Its card says it hands mail to
   WordPress's own mail function with no account needed. If another SMTP plugin, such as WP Mail SMTP, FluentSMTP or
   Post SMTP, should send your site's mail, choose this one. The others are named for how AccessBay reaches them, for
   example **Twilio SendGrid (API)**, **Mailgun (API)** and **SMTP2GO (API)**.
4. Fill in the form. It has groups: **Sending identity** (**Name**, **From address**, **From name**; the last two are
   optional), **Connection**, **Credentials** and, for providers that report delivery, **Webhook**. **Back** returns
   to the list of services.
5. Select **Save and test**. AccessBay saves the provider and runs a connection test. If the test fails, the dialog
   stays open and shows the reason, so you can fix the fields and try again. **Save** stores the provider without a
   test.

The **Status**, **Last check** and **Last test** columns of the table show the results.

AccessBay stores keys, tokens and passwords encrypted and never shows them again. To change one, open the provider
with **Edit** and enter the new value.

Each provider also needs its sender or sending domain verified in the provider's own account. Without that, the
provider can refuse to send.

You can add as many providers as you like. Each has its own page with the steps to get its key and the values to enter:

- [Twilio SendGrid](/guide/providers/sendgrid/)
- [Mailgun](/guide/providers/mailgun/)
- [Postmark](/guide/providers/postmark/)
- [Resend](/guide/providers/resend/)
- [Brevo](/guide/providers/brevo/)
- [SMTP2GO](/guide/providers/smtp2go/)
- [ZeptoMail](/guide/providers/zeptomail/)
- [SMTP](/guide/providers/smtp/), including Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 and your host's mail server
- [WordPress (wp_mail)](/guide/providers/wp-mail/)

[Email providers](/guide/providers/overview/) helps you choose one.

## Test a provider

There are two tests. Both are buttons in the **Actions** column of the Email providers table.

- **Test connection** checks the provider's key or login. For most types it sends no email. ZeptoMail and SMTP2GO
  can't check without sending, so for them it sends a test email to your own admin address.
- **Send test email** (the send button in the row) opens a dialog titled "Send a test email via" the provider's name.
  The **Send to** field starts with your own address, and you can use any address. It sends one short test email
  through that provider only. If it fails,
  no other provider takes over. AccessBay refuses an address on the Suppressions list. Each admin can send 10 an
  hour, and the whole site has a cap per hour as well. The email shows in the Email log as a test.

If a test fails because of the address, the rate limit or a refused message, the provider's health stays as it was.

## Webhooks

A webhook lets a provider tell AccessBay what happened to an email after it accepted it: delivered, bounced or
complained about. Without it, the email stays at "Sent".

For every provider that supports webhooks, the Email providers screen has a **Webhooks** card. It shows a **Webhook
URL** for that provider with a copy button. Paste it into the provider's webhook settings, then enter the matching
secret in AccessBay as described on the provider's page. AccessBay refuses a webhook that fails the check.

`wp_mail`, SMTP and ZeptoMail have no webhook.

## How failover, retries and alerts work

**Order.** AccessBay tries the providers in the order of the table. Use the **Move up** and **Move down** buttons to
change it. The first provider that accepts the email wins.

**Failover.** If a provider fails, AccessBay tries the next one straight away. After three failures in ten minutes,
AccessBay pauses that provider for five minutes. The pause doubles each time up to an hour, and the **Status** column
shows "Paused until" the time. A provider is also paused at once if its key is refused or its account is suspended. It is
tried again after you change its settings or **Test connection** passes. If its credits or quota run out, it is
paused until the provider resets them or for an hour, and AccessBay records an alert at once. Each time a
provider goes down or recovers, AccessBay records one alert.

**Retries.** If every provider fails, AccessBay tries the whole list again after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 15 minutes, 1
hour, 3 hours, 6 hours, 12 hours and then daily. It stops after the **Email retry period** in Settings > Email, which
is 3 days by default and can be 1 to 5. The first time every provider fails, AccessBay records an alert, once per outage. When the retry
period is spent, the email is marked failed and an alert is recorded.

**A bad address.** If a provider says the address itself can't receive mail, AccessBay doesn't try other providers.
It marks the email failed and adds the address to the Suppressions list.

**When the outcome is unknown.** If a connection drops after the email was sent, AccessBay can't tell whether the
provider took it. Brevo and Resend accept a repeat of the same email safely, so AccessBay asks the same provider
again. For the other providers, AccessBay marks the email "Possible duplicate" and carries on with the next round,
because a duplicate email is better than a lost licence email.

**Site Health.** The "AccessBay email delivery" check warns when `wp_mail` is your only provider, a provider is
paused or failed its last test, a provider's credits ran out, a provider with a webhook has reported nothing for 7
days although it accepted email, an email failed every retry, or the primary provider or the site's own mail failed
in the last 24 hours.

## Monitoring and alerts

**What is checked.** Once an hour AccessBay checks every enabled provider. If a provider can check its credentials
without sending, AccessBay does that. `wp_mail` and the providers that can't (ZeptoMail and SMTP2GO) are judged from
their real sends. The **Status** and **Last check** columns of the Email providers table show the result. The
**Monitoring and alerts** card shows when the last check ran and when the next one runs.

**Daily test send.** It is off by default, because it sends real email. To turn it on, switch on **Send a daily test
email** in Settings > Email. AccessBay then sends a short test email through each provider once a day. It goes to
**Daily test email recipient**, or to the site administrator if that is empty. The Site Health check warns if a
provider refuses it.

**Who is told.** When a provider goes from working to failing, AccessBay shows a notice on its own screens and emails
the addresses in **Mail problem alerts** in Settings > Email. Enter up to ten, separated by commas or new lines. If
it is empty, the email goes to the site administrator. It is sent through a provider that works, never the failing
one, or through plain `wp_mail()` if none does. While the problem lasts, AccessBay sends one reminder every 24 hours
at most. When the provider works again, it sends one more email. If every enabled provider fails, that counts as its
own problem, and it closes when one provider works again.

**The notice.** A red box at the top of the Email providers screen says "Email delivery has a problem" (or "Email
delivery has problems" when there are several) and lists each affected provider.

Addresses in error text, alerts and alert emails are masked, for example `j***@example.com`. A staging copy holds
alerts under its send guard instead of emailing them.

## The email log

Go to AccessBay > Email log. It has three tabs, **AccessBay email**, **All site email** and **Suppressions**.

- **AccessBay email** lists every email AccessBay sends, with its status. Open one to see its **Attempts** (each
  provider tried, the result and how long it took) and its **Provider events** (delivered, bounced and so on). Use
  **Retry** to put a failed or held email back in the queue, **Cancel email** to stop one that is waiting, and
  **Resend** to send a new copy. A resend is built again from current data, and the original stays in the log.
- **All site email** lists every email your site sends with `wp_mail`, from any plugin, with its recipient, subject,
  time and result.
- **Suppressions** lists addresses AccessBay won't send to: those that bounced or complained, and those added by
  hand. **Lift suppression** removes one.

The logs keep recipients, subjects, times and results. They don't keep the body of any email.

### Filtering the logs

Each log has its own filters in one row above the table. Each filter button shows its choice, for example "Status:
Failed, Bounced". A filter that allows several values opens a menu of checkboxes that stays open while you tick, and a
row matches when it has any ticked value. **Clear filters** appears when any filter is set and puts them all back.

- **AccessBay email:** **Status** (Queued, Held, Accepted, Suppressed, Failed, Cancelled, Bounced), **Delivery**
  (Deferred, Delivered, Bounced, Complained) and **Provider** (one provider, or all). The table shows the recipient,
  the template (with a "Possible duplicate" badge when it applies), the status, whether the provider reported
  delivery, the provider and the number of attempts. Where a provider can't report delivery, the delivery column says
  so, for example "Sent; delivery not reported by this provider".
- **All site email:** a **Search recipients** box and a **Result** filter (Sent, Failed). The table shows the recipient,
  subject, time, result and any error.

Use **Load more** under the table to see older rows. These filters are not part of the page address and you can't
save them as views, unlike the lists on other screens ([Search and filters](/guide/finding-things/)).

### Retention

AccessBay keeps all of it by default. In Settings > Email, **Email record retention** is 0, which means keep
everything. Enter a number of days to delete older AccessBay emails, their attempts, provider events and site-mail
log entries. An email still waiting to be sent is never deleted.

### Privacy export and erase

AccessBay adds a person's emails to the WordPress personal data exporter and eraser under Tools. The export covers
the mail log entries, attempts, provider events, site-mail log entries and suppressions for the person's address.
The eraser deletes emails that were never sent and replaces the address in the rest with a placeholder. It keeps
ids, status and timing. A suppressed address stays suppressed.

## Search and filters
URL: https://docs.wpanchorbay.com/accessbay/guide/finding-things/
Description: How to use AccessBay's search dialog, the filter row on list screens, saved views, and shareable links.

AccessBay has two ways to find something. The search dialog looks across the whole plugin. The filter row narrows the
list you are looking at.

## The search dialog

Open it with the **Search** box in the sidebar, or press `/` on any AccessBay screen. The `/` key does nothing while
your cursor is in a text field, and it ignores the Ctrl, Cmd and Alt keys, so it never takes over a shortcut of your
browser.

Type at least two characters. AccessBay waits a moment after you stop typing, then shows the results in groups:
Licences, Customers, Orders, Products, and Settings and dashboard. Each group shows up to eight results, and Settings
and dashboard up to twelve. The status line
under the field says how many results there are, or "No results".

- Press the up and down arrow keys to move through the results.
- Press Enter to open the highlighted one. If none is highlighted, Enter opens the first.
- Press Escape to close the dialog.

### What it searches

| Group | You can search by |
|---|---|
| Licences | The licence's id, the last four characters of its key, or a whole key pasted in |
| Customers | The customer's id, or the start of an email address, last name or company |
| Orders | The order's id, the exact order number, or the start of the buyer's email address |
| Products | The product's id, or any part of its name or slug |
| Settings and dashboard | Words from the name or help text of a setting, a settings section or a dashboard panel |

A pasted licence key is searched for and never saved. The dialog sends it in the body of the request, never in the
page address, and a licence result shows only the last four characters of the key. Customers that were merged into
another customer don't show up.

### Settings in the results

Search also finds settings, so "retention" takes you to the retention fields without you knowing which section holds
them. It covers every settings section and each field in it, the API keys screen, the Email providers screen, the
Danger zone and the dashboard panels. It matches the label and the help text of a field. It never looks at the value
you saved.

A result shows where it lives, for example "Settings > Email settings". A field result opens its section, scrolls to
the field and puts the cursor in it. Every word you type has to match, so a longer search gives fewer results. Label
matches come before help-text matches, and there are at most twelve settings results.

Only people who may manage AccessBay's settings see settings results. Everyone else sees the dashboard results only.

## The filter row on list screens

Products, Orders, Licences, Activations and Customers share one layout: a single row above the table, then the table,
then the pager.

- **Search box.** Searches that list only. AccessBay waits a moment after you stop typing. Press Escape to empty the
  box. What it searches depends on the screen, and the placeholder text says so.
- **Filter buttons.** One button per filter. The button shows its name and your choice, for example "Status: Active,
  Draft", or "Status: All" when nothing is chosen. When the choice is long, the button says "3 selected" instead.
- **Clear filters.** Appears only when a search or a filter is set. It empties them all in one step.
- **Save view.** Appears when the list differs from its default and is not already a saved view. See below.
- **Views.** Appears once you have saved a view. See below.
- **Columns.** The columns button lists the columns with a checkbox each, so you can hide the ones you don't need.

A filter can take more than one value. Its menu is a list of checkboxes that stays open while you tick, so you can
choose "Active" and "Draft" in one visit. A row matches a filter when it has any of the ticked values. Different
filters combine: "Status: Active" and "Type: Software" shows only the rows that are both.
